The slow return of the night train

For years the overnight sleeper was written off as a relic. Airlines undercut it on price, and motorways drew away the commuters who once filled its carriages. Yet a handful of stubborn operators kept a few routes alive.

Their patience is now paying off. Travellers who care about the climate are rediscovering the simple pleasure of falling asleep in one city and waking up in another, without airport queues or security lines.

Rolling stock remains the biggest obstacle. Many compartments date from the nineteen seventies, and manufacturers need several years to deliver new sleeping cars even when orders are placed promptly.

Still, the mood has changed. Ministries that once talked about closing lines now speak about timetables, ticket prices and the cross-border agreements needed to make a continental network work smoothly.

Passengers describe the experience in modest terms. A narrow bunk, a cup of tea and the muffled rhythm of the rails are, apparently, all they ask for.
